newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to start Latin America trip in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to start Latin America trip in Mexico.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton heads to Mexico Monday to start a week-long Latin America trip designed to strengthen U.S. bonds to the region while dealing with such concerns as immigration and drug-smuggling.
After a morning of private briefings on the trip from foreign policy advisers, Clinton was to depart for Mexico City mid-afternoon for his first visit to the U.S. neighbour as president.

"An important opportunity exists for the United States to build closer relations with the government of Mexico and continue our efforts of cooperation on a number of issues," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.

The first U.S. president to visit the Mexican capital since Jimmy Carter in 1979, Clinton also was scheduled to participate in a Central American summit in Costa Rica and a Caribbean summit in Barbados.
Cabinet officials and senior administration officials were already in Mexico to meet with their counterparts on a broad range of issues.
Although Clinton waited until the fifth year of his presidency to visit Mexico, he has already established solid credentials with its government.

In 1995 he ignored congressional critics and devised an emergency rescue plan that helped Mexico emerge from its peso crisis. The year before, he overcame strong opposition and convinced a reluctant Congress to approve the North American Free Trade Agreement, which also includes Canada.

The visit to Mexico comes at a time of strained relations fuelled by Washington's complaints about corruption among high-level Mexican drug agents and the country's efforts to stem the flow of illegal drugs entering the United States.

Although Washington estimates that 70 percent of illegal drugs enter the United States from Mexico, U.S. officials expect only modest agreements on increased cooperation on the drug war to come from the visit.
Mexico, on the other hand, is upset with new U.S. immigration laws cracking down on illegal immigrants that its leaders fear will lead to mass deportations.

Clinton intends to use his visit to defuse those concerns. "We are going to work very hard to avoid any Draconian interpretation of the law that would lead to any kind of mass deportations or anything of that kind," he said in an interview with CNN Radio Noticias.
One long-standing dispute that Clinton would like to resolve is whether agents from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency can carry their guns while in Mexico.
U.S. officials asked for permission after murders in late 1996 of Mexican officers who had been working with U.S. agents.
